title: Expressions and arithmetic
summary: Combine values, make grouping clear, and understand why the operand types matter.
objectives: Predict small arithmetic expressions using precedence and parentheses.
Distinguish integer division from floating-point division and calculate a remainder.
Explain assignment updates and recognize the limits of built-in arithmetic.

blocks.text: An expression combines values and operations to perform a computation. A literal such as 5 is an expression; so is a variable name used to read its value. With two small integers, 5 + 2 computes another integer. The values an operator works on are its operands. For + in that expression, the operands are 5 and 2.

The familiar arithmetic operators are + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. C++ uses % for an integer remainder, which you will examine next. A calculation can initialize a named result or appear directly in an output statement. Giving an intermediate result a name can make its purpose easier to explain.

blocks.caption: arithmetic.cpp — a complete C++20 program
Expected standard output
blocks.code:
Total pages: 15
Without grouping: 14
With grouping: 20

blocks.text: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so 2 + 3 * 4 groups as 2 + (3 * 4). Parentheses change the grouping in (2 + 3) * 4. Operators such as subtraction group left to right at the same precedence: 10 - 3 - 2 means (10 - 3) - 2. Use parentheses when they make your intention easier to see.

blocks.title: Grouping is one question
blocks.text: Precedence describes how an expression is grouped. It is not a general rule for the order in which every part of a more complicated expression executes. These examples only read values. Keep updates in separate statements while learning to reason about expressions.

Work an expression from its grouping and operand types toward its result. In pagesPerDay * days, both named values are small integers, so multiplying 5 by 3 produces the integer 15. The const on totalPages prevents a later ordinary assignment to that result; it does not change the multiplication rule. The name adds meaning: the multiplication combines pages per day with a number of days, leaving a page count. Keeping units in names helps expose mistakes that the built-in integer type cannot distinguish.

For 2 + 3 * 4, first write the implicit grouping as 2 + (3 * 4). The inner multiplication yields 12, then addition yields 14. For (2 + 3) * 4, the explicitly grouped addition yields 5, then multiplication yields 20. The difference is not a formatting issue. Parentheses change the expression being computed. A useful debugging technique is to replace a complicated calculation with named intermediate results whose meanings and values can be checked separately.

blocks.prompt: A learner says 12 - 4 - 2 should be 10 because 4 - 2 is 2. Identify the missing reasoning step and compute both possible groupings.
blocks.explanation: The written expression groups as (12 - 4) - 2, giving 8 - 2 = 6. The learner evaluated 12 - (4 - 2), which requires explicit parentheses and gives 10. Determine the grouping before computing the numbers. This example uses pure reads, so it teaches associativity without introducing side effects or assumptions about operand evaluation order.

blocks.text: When both operands are integers, division produces an integer quotient with the fractional part discarded toward zero. Therefore 7 / 2 is 3, and -7 / 2 is -3. This is not rounding to the nearest integer. The % operator supplies the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1 because three groups of two leave one.

blocks.caption: division.cpp — a complete C++20 program
Expected standard output
blocks.code:
Whole groups: 3
Left over: 1
Fractional: 3.5
Converted after: 3

blocks.text: The literal 7.0 has type double. In 7.0 / 2, the integer operand is converted to double before the division, so the calculation can produce 3.5. In contrast, convertedAfter receives the result of integer division. Storing that result in a double cannot recover the discarded fraction. First examine the expression’s operands, then the destination type.

blocks.prompt: If both 7s in the integer calculations became 8, what would wholeGroups and leftOver contain?
blocks.explanation: wholeGroups would contain 4 and leftOver would contain 0: four groups of two use all eight items. Predict both values together. The quotient counts complete groups and the remainder tells you what remains, for these nonnegative integers and this positive divisor.

blocks.text: Integer division answers a different question from fractional division. Given seven pages and groups of two pages, the integer quotient counts three complete groups. The remainder records the one page not assigned to those complete groups. Together they reconstruct the original quantity: 3 times 2 plus 1 equals 7. This reconstruction is a useful independent check on a quotient-and-remainder calculation; it is stronger than remembering one expected number.

blocks.caption: Second worked case — quotient and remainder with a negative dividend
blocks.code:
Assume representable int operands and a nonzero divisor.
-7 / 2 -> -3, because truncation is toward zero
-7 % 2 -> -1
Reconstruct: (-3) * 2 + (-1) = -7
Rounding downward to -4 would describe a different division rule.

blocks.text: The negative example prevents an easy overgeneralization from positive inputs. C++ integer division discards the fractional part toward zero, so its result for -3.5 is -3 rather than -4. For a representable quotient, the quotient and remainder satisfy the reconstruction identity. If your application needs mathematical floor division or a nonnegative modular index, you need an explicitly designed calculation instead of assuming that / and % already implement that convention.

The order of conversion is the central lesson of convertedAfter. The initializer first computes 7 / 2 as an integer expression, obtaining 3. Only then is 3 represented in the destination double. The fractional information was never present in that result. In 7.0 / 2 the common operand type changes before division, so 3.5 is available. A destination with more precision cannot repair a lossy earlier operation.

Assignment stores a computed result. With an ordinary int variable pages already initialized to 5, the statement pages = pages + 2; reads the old value, adds two, then stores seven. For this simple variable, pages += 2; expresses the same update more compactly. The single = means assignment; it is not the equality comparison operator ==.

Built-in arithmetic has limits. An int has a finite range, and overflowing a signed integer does not promise a wrapped result. Integer division or remainder with a zero divisor has undefined behavior. Neither situation has a portable result you can rely on. The small, nonzero examples here stay within their types’ ranges; larger programs must check the values they accept and calculate.

Floating-point values also have finite precision. Many familiar decimal fractions, such as 0.1 on common binary floating-point implementations, cannot be represented exactly. Our example uses 3.5 to keep the result simple. For now, practice with small values: predict the type, add parentheses to show the grouping, calculate the result, and only then compile and compare the output.

Assignment is a state transition, not an algebraic equation. In pages = pages + 2, the right side uses the value from before the assignment and the left side identifies the object to change. Starting at 5, the successive statements pages += 2 and pages += 2 produce 7 and then 9. Evaluating the same update twice therefore has a different effect from merely reading an expression twice. Keep updates visible as separate statements until you can explain both the values computed and the state changed.

Check dangerous operations before evaluating them. Discovering afterward that a divisor was zero does not undo undefined behavior. Likewise, choosing a larger destination type does not guarantee that multiplication performed in a smaller signed operand type was representable. The small examples intentionally avoid these hazards; the next modules teach conditions and interfaces that let you make such preconditions explicit. For division there is also a signed boundary case when the mathematical quotient is not representable, even with a nonzero divisor.

Use a four-column paper trace for a new calculation: intended quantity and units, operand types and grouping, intermediate numeric results, and the state after assignment. For the daily-pages example the columns identify pages, int multiplication, 15, and an unchanged source pair with a newly initialized result. This connects arithmetic to program state and prepares you to put calculations behind conditions and inside functions without losing track of when information is read or changed.

blocks.prompt: Nine items are shared between four groups. Predict 9 / 4, 9 % 4, and 9.0 / 4. Which result answers “complete items per group,” and which answers “fractional average”?
blocks.explanation: The integer quotient is 2 and remainder is 1 because 2 times 4 plus 1 equals 9. The floating calculation is 2.25. Use the quotient when items are indivisible and keep the remainder as part of the result; use a fractional average when a fractional quantity is meaningful. These are different questions, so choosing an operator or type begins with the application requirement.
